# Supabase Security: File Uploads Done Properly

A photograph taken on a phone carries the coordinates where it was taken. Most people know this vaguely. Very few founders realise that their app has been publishing those coordinates, because the generated upload feature stored the file exactly as it arrived and served it to anyone with the address.

Uploads look like the simplest feature in a product: a button, a file, a URL. They are one of the densest concentrations of risk in a small application, because they combine untrusted input, permanent storage, public serving and unbounded cost in a single interaction. Here is what a properly built one actually involves.

## Four Questions Every Upload Feature Must Answer

Before any implementation detail: what types are accepted, how large may they be, who may read them afterwards, and when are they removed. An AI-generated upload feature typically answers "anything", "any size", "anyone with the link" and "never".

Each of those four defaults is a separate problem, and they compound: an unrestricted file, stored at a guessable address, readable without authentication, forever.

## Validate on the Server, Because the Browser Is Not Yours

Browser-side checks — the accept attribute on a file input, a JavaScript check on the extension — are user interface conveniences. Anyone can call your upload endpoint directly with whatever they like.

Real validation happens on the server and checks three things: the actual content type rather than the file extension, which is trivially renamed; the file size against a limit you set; and, for images, that the file genuinely decodes as an image rather than merely claiming to be one.

The specific risk worth naming is a file that is not what it says it is, served from your own domain. Content served from your domain inherits your domain's trust, which is why "we only accept images" needs to be enforced where it cannot be bypassed.

## Storage Layout and Names Nobody Can Guess

Two decisions here have outsized consequences.

**Never use the uploaded filename.** It may collide with another user's file, may contain characters that cause problems in a path, and — most importantly — it is predictable. Generate a random identifier and store the original name separately as metadata if you need to display it.

**Organise by owner.** A path structure that includes the account or organisation identifier makes access rules simple to express and simple to verify. Files scattered in one flat bucket make every access decision a special case.

Combined, these mean that even if a file becomes readable, it is not enumerable. Someone who obtains one address learns nothing about the next one — which is precisely what fails when files are named `invoice-1.pdf` through `invoice-400.pdf`.

## Private by Default, Signed When Needed

The single most important setting: buckets holding user content should be private, not public.

Access then happens through signed URLs — temporary addresses your server generates for a specific file, for a specific requester, expiring after a defined period. The expiry matters: a signed URL pasted into an email or a support ticket stops working, whereas a public URL circulates indefinitely.

Before generating one, your server checks whether this user may see this file. That check is the entire security model, and it is the step generated code omits, because in the demo the only person uploading was the developer.

## Metadata: What Files Carry Without Telling You

Photographs from phones and cameras commonly embed capture coordinates, timestamps, device model and sometimes the owner's name. Documents from office software carry author names, revision history and occasionally text that was deleted but not removed.

For most products the right default is to strip metadata on upload for images, keeping only what you need such as orientation. For documents, be aware that the file you serve contains more than the page shows — and if your product handles documents between parties who should not know everything about each other, that is a matter to design for rather than discover.

This is not theoretical. A marketplace serving original photographs publishes sellers' home coordinates to anyone who downloads a listing image.

## Malware, Proportionately

Should a small product scan uploads for malware? The honest answer depends on what happens to the files.

If uploads are only ever viewed by the person who uploaded them, the risk is largely theirs. If files are shared between users — a document exchange, a marketplace, anything where one person's upload reaches another's device — then you are a distribution mechanism, and scanning becomes appropriate.

For most small products the proportionate measures are: strict type restrictions, serving files with headers that force download rather than execution where appropriate, never executing uploaded content, and adding scanning when files move between users. A full security programme is not required to do the first three.

## Quotas, Because Storage Is Not Free

An upload feature without a limit is an open invitation, and the cost appears in two places: storage, which accumulates, and bandwidth, which recurs every time a file is served.

Set a per-file size limit and a per-account total. Decide what happens at the limit — refuse, or offer an upgrade — and communicate it in the interface rather than in an error. And remember that serving is usually the larger cost: a popular listing with large photographs generates far more bandwidth than the storage figure suggests.

This is also where the image pipeline pays for itself. Generating display-sized versions at upload and serving those instead of originals typically reduces bandwidth by an order of magnitude.

## Deletion and the Orphans Nobody Sees

When a user deletes a listing, a profile or a message, does the associated file disappear?

In most AI-built apps, no. The database row is removed and the file remains, unreferenced, billed monthly, forever. Over a year this accumulates into a meaningful share of storage — and, more seriously, files that should have been deleted at a user's request remain retrievable by anyone who kept the address.

Two things to build: deletion of files when their owning record is deleted, and a periodic job that finds files with no corresponding record and removes them. Run the second once against your existing data; the result is frequently surprising.

## A Checklist Before Launch

- Type and size validated on the server, with content inspected rather than trusted.
- Random file names, organised by owner.
- Buckets private, access through expiring signed URLs after an authorisation check.
- Image metadata stripped on upload.
- Display-sized versions generated; originals kept only if needed.
- Per-account quotas with a clear message at the limit.
- Deletion cascades from records to files, plus an orphan cleanup.
- A test: upload a file renamed to a permitted extension, and confirm it is rejected.

## Serving Files: The Half That Happens After Upload

Upload hardening gets the attention; delivery is where the cost and most of the perceived slowness live.

**Serve derivatives, not originals.** Generate the sizes your interface displays at upload time and serve those. This is usually the single largest reduction in bandwidth available to a small product, and it improves mobile load time at the same time.

**Use modern formats with a fallback.** Current image formats produce substantially smaller files at equivalent quality, and browsers that cannot handle them can be given the older version.

**Cache aggressively, with immutable names.** Because your file names are random and never reused, a file at a given address never changes — which means it can be cached for a long time. If a user replaces their photograph, they get a new address rather than a stale cached copy.

**Put a content delivery network in front of storage** once you have users outside your own region. It reduces both latency and egress from your origin.

**Lazy-load below the fold.** A listing page with thirty images should not download thirty images before showing anything.

**Remember signed URLs and caching interact.** An expiring URL cannot be cached for longer than it is valid, so for genuinely public assets a public, cacheable path is appropriate, while private files trade some caching efficiency for access control. Decide which category each file belongs to rather than applying one rule to everything.

## Real example

### A Marketplace That Published Its Sellers' Home Addresses

Ravi Mehta built Vintagehoek in Lovable: a marketplace for second-hand furniture in and around Haarlem. Sellers photographed items at home and listed them; buyers browsed and arranged collection.

Three findings, in ascending order of seriousness. Storage costs were four times what the listing count suggested, because photographs were stored at full camera resolution and served the same way, and because deleted listings never removed their images. Files were named from the upload, so addresses were guessable. And the bucket was public with original photographs intact, including embedded capture coordinates — meaning anyone could download a listing image and read the seller's home location, including for listings that had been deleted months earlier.

The seller who reported it had found her own address by opening her photograph's details.

Six business days of work: metadata stripped on upload; an image pipeline producing thumbnail, card and detail sizes with originals discarded; bucket made private with signed URLs expiring after fifteen minutes, issued only after an authorisation check; random file names organised per seller; deletion cascaded from listings to files; an orphan cleanup run once historically, removing roughly 40% of stored data; and per-account quotas introduced.

**Result:** storage and bandwidth costs fell by roughly three-quarters, listing pages loaded in under a second on mobile, and the coordinates exposure was closed for both new and existing photographs.

> *"A seller emailed me her own home address and asked how my website knew it. That was how I found out my app had been publishing it for nine months."*
> — **Ravi Mehta, Founder, Vintagehoek (Haarlem)**

**Cost & Timeline:** €2,650 (upload validation, metadata stripping, image pipeline, signed access, cleanup of existing files) — completed in 6 business days.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is checking the file extension enough validation?

No. Extensions are trivially renamed. Validate the actual content type on the server, confirm images genuinely decode as images, and enforce a size limit where the browser cannot bypass it.

### Should my storage bucket be public or private?

Private, for anything users upload. Serve files through expiring signed URLs generated after your server has checked that this requester may see this file. Public buckets mean anyone with an address has permanent access.

### What metadata do I need to strip?

For photographs, capture coordinates, timestamps and device details, keeping orientation if you need it. Documents also carry author names and revision history, which matters when files move between parties.

### Do I need virus scanning?

If files are only seen by their uploader, rarely. If files are shared between users, you are a distribution mechanism and scanning becomes appropriate — alongside strict type restrictions and never executing uploaded content.

### Why is my storage bill higher than my file count suggests?

Almost always originals stored at full resolution and orphaned files from deleted records. Generating display sizes and running an orphan cleanup typically removes a large share of stored data in one pass.
